meta.blurb: Mei snoozes, scrolls in the dark and starts every day already behind. Kofi works nights, and Elena has a toddler. None of them needs a perfect routine, only a short, realistic first hour that fits a real life.
meta.bible: Mei: an accountant who used to snooze, scroll and rush, and now builds a calm first hour. Kofi: a nurse who works night shifts, so his first hour comes after he wakes in the afternoon. Elena: a parent of a toddler who keeps her routine tiny. The book speaks to "you" and uses these three as examples. World Health Organization: its guidance for adults is at least one hundred and fifty minutes of moderate activity a week. Facts are real and hedged: body clocks differ, adults generally need at least seven hours of sleep, research on snoozing is mixed, slow breathing, meditation and gratitude show modest benefits in some studies, picturing the steps helps more than picturing only the result, habit formation varies from person to person. This is not a diet, a treatment or a promise of a miracle. Voice and tone: warm, honest, practical and gentle, one clear idea or step in each beat, building to a final takeaway. Extended cast: Dana, Mei's friend from the office, who becomes her partner in the habit. Mateo, Elena's son, aged two. Omar, Elena's husband, who leaves early for work. Joy, a nurse who works with Kofi on the night ward. Sundays are Mei's slow mornings. Mei's notebook is small and green. Her kettle stands by the window. The first-hour recipe in this book: water, light, movement, quiet, writing, learning, a plan and one small step. Beginners start with ten minutes. Mei's father goes into hospital for a week in her second month. Mei sits her professional accounting exam in the spring and passes. Mei is learning Spanish and studying for that exam; Dana writes a children's story for her niece.

B1B2: For many people, the first minutes of the day belong to the phone. Messages, news and other people's demands arrive before the person is even awake.
Mei used to press snooze three times, check her phone and then rush out of the door. She arrived at work already tired, with her toast still in her hand.
Before she has even brushed her teeth, Mei has read three work messages and a worrying headline. Her heart is already beating faster, and she has not yet put her feet on the floor.
By the middle of the afternoon, Mei is drinking her third coffee and staring at the same spreadsheet. In the evening she is too tired to do anything except scroll again.
One Sunday there is no alarm, and Mei wakes slowly while the sun creeps into the room. She drinks her tea by the window, and for once nothing is chasing her.
At lunch on Monday, her friend Dana says that Mei looks tired and asks how she is sleeping. Mei laughs and admits that her mornings are a mess.
Dana explains that she spends ten quiet minutes each morning with a cup of tea and a notebook, before she touches her phone. It is not magic, she says, but it helps her feel ready.
Mei shakes her head and says that she is simply not a morning person. Dana smiles and answers that nobody has to become one, because the aim is a calmer start and not an early one.
On her way home Mei buys a small green notebook and a box of tea. She makes a modest promise to herself: ten minutes each morning for one week, and then she will decide.
This book has one simple idea, and it is easy to say. Choose how your first hour will go, and use it to start the day in a way that you would like.
Let us be honest with each other from the start. People have different body clocks, and getting up very early does not suit everyone.

Some people naturally wake early and feel best in the morning, while others come alive late at night. Scientists think this difference is partly inherited, so it is not simply a question of willpower.
The first hour in this book is not tied to the clock on the wall. It begins whenever you wake up, whether that is at five in the morning or at three in the afternoon.
Meet Kofi, a nurse who works the night shift on a busy hospital ward. He goes to bed when most people are waking up, so his mornings arrive in the afternoon.
Meet Elena, whose son Mateo is two years old and wakes before the sun every day. Her mornings belong to him, and she cannot imagine finding a quiet hour in them.
Throughout this book, Mei, Kofi and Elena will show you three different ways to build a first hour. Their lives are very different, but they all want the same thing, which is a calmer start.

A first hour can contain a number of small parts: water, light, movement, quiet, writing, learning, a plan and one small step. You will meet each of them in turn, and you are free to use only the ones that suit you.
There is one rule in this book, and it is a kind one. Take the parts that suit you, leave the others, and never feel guilty about what you leave behind.
Ten minutes is enough to count as a real first hour, at least when you are beginning. A small routine that you keep is worth far more than a grand one that you abandon after three days.
Before she starts, Mei writes down what she wants from her mornings. She chooses three words in her green notebook: calm, time and choice.
A good morning really starts on the night before it. Health organisations say that most adults need at least seven hours of sleep, although the exact amount differs from person to person.
Mei counts the hours between her bedtime and her alarm, and the answer surprises her. She gets about six hours on most nights, which is less than she thought.
Going to bed and getting up at similar times helps your body clock to settle. It does not have to be exact, but big changes from one day to the next make mornings harder.
An hour before bed, Mei dims the lights and puts her phone on a shelf far away. The quiet gives her tired mind plenty of time to slow down.
Caffeine stays in your body for many hours, so a coffee late in the afternoon can still be working at bedtime. Mei decides to stop drinking coffee after lunch and sees how she sleeps.
A very heavy meal late in the evening can make it harder to settle down. Alcohol may help you fall asleep at first, but it often makes your sleep lighter later in the night.
Many sleep experts suggest a bedroom that is dark, quiet and a little cool. Mei hangs a heavier curtain over the window, and she turns off the small light on her laptop.
Mei often lies awake because her mind keeps listing tomorrow's jobs. So before bed she writes them on a sheet of paper, and some small studies suggest this can help people fall asleep.
Sometimes sleep simply does not come, and that happens to everyone. If you have been awake for a long time, get up, do something quiet in dim light and return to bed when you feel sleepy.
On Sunday night Mei turns off her lamp at half past ten, and she wakes just before the alarm rings. She still feels a little sleepy, but it is a much kinder kind of sleepy.
Before bed, Mei puts a glass of water, a set of clean clothes and her notebook on a chair. Tomorrow's first minutes will be easier because tonight has already done some of the work.
Mei also packs her bag, finds her keys and puts everything beside the front door. The old morning search for lost things, which used to make her late, simply disappears.
Mei used to keep her phone under her pillow, so the snooze button was always within reach. Now she puts the alarm across the room, which means she has to stand up to turn it off.
Mei changes her harsh, loud alarm to a soft piece of music that begins quietly and slowly grows. A pleasant sound is a kinder first message to send to a sleepy brain.
On the first morning, the alarm plays, and Mei groans, swings her legs out of bed and walks across the room. She is not happy about it, but she is up, and that is the hardest part.
Mei leaves her phone on the dresser and goes to the window instead. She gives herself a few quiet minutes before the world is allowed to reach her.
Pressing snooze feels lovely for nine minutes, but then you must wake up anyway. The research on snoozing is mixed, yet one clear wake-up is simpler and leaves no room for argument.
Mei writes one small reason to get up on a card by her bed. It is nothing grand, just a hot cup of tea by the window, but a pleasant reward helps her feet reach the floor.
Mei makes her bed before she does anything else, and it takes about a minute. It is a tiny job, but it gives her a first small success and a tidier room to return to.
On the second morning, Mei feels just as tired, and the bed looks even more inviting than before. She stands up anyway, because she made a promise and a promise is easier to keep when it is small.
The first thing Mei does is open the curtains and let the daylight in. Morning light helps to set your body clock, and it tells your brain that the day has begun.
Even on a grey and cloudy day, the light outdoors is far brighter than the light in most rooms. That is why a few minutes by an open window or outside the door can matter.
In winter it can still be dark when Mei wakes, so she turns on a bright lamp in the kitchen. Some people use special light lamps, and anyone whose winter mood is very low should talk to a doctor.
After the curtains, Mei pours a tall glass of water and drinks it slowly by the window. She has not had a drink for hours, and it feels like a small and sensible kindness.
Nothing in this book is against coffee, and you do not have to give up your favourite morning drink. Mei simply drinks a glass of water first, then enjoys her coffee with more attention.
Next Mei washes her face and puts on her clean clothes. Her body knows that these small actions mean the day has begun, even if the sky is still dark.
Some people work from home and are tempted to stay in their pyjamas all day. Dressing for the day, even in comfortable clothes, can help you feel ready and mark the line between rest and work.
Standing at the window with her water, Mei begins to notice things she never saw before. She sees the colour of the sky, a neighbour's cat on a wall and small birds on the wire.
After a few days, the first three steps run together without any effort. Curtains, water and a wash take Mei about seven minutes, and she no longer has to think about them.
Mei looks at the clock and sees that twenty minutes have passed since she woke up. She has not checked her phone or thought about work, and she feels surprisingly calm.
After her wash, Mei unrolls a mat beside her bed and moves her body for a few minutes. She does not push hard, because the aim is to wake up and not to punish herself.

Her routine is made of three easy moves: reach both arms up high, roll the shoulders slowly and bend gently forward. If anything hurts, she stops, because stretching should feel pleasant and never painful.
Even a single minute of movement can help your body feel more awake after hours of lying still. If you have only a tiny window of time, spend it on moving.
The World Health Organization suggests that adults aim for at least one hundred and fifty minutes of moderate activity a week. That is a general guide, and any amount of movement is better than none.
On the fourth morning, Mei walks for ten minutes along her quiet street. A short walk outside gives her daylight and movement at the same time, which is a bargain.
Mei does the sums and is pleased with the result. Ten minutes a day, for seven days, comes to seventy minutes, which is already nearly half of the weekly guide.
How fast should you walk or move for it to count as moderate? A common rule is that you should be able to talk but not sing a whole song.
Health guidelines also suggest that adults strengthen their muscles on at least two days a week. Mei begins very gently with five slow stands from a chair, and she counts them aloud.
If you have a heart problem, an injury, a long illness or a pregnancy, speak to a doctor before you begin. Everyone should start slowly and build up, and no routine is worth hurting yourself for.
By the end of the week, Mei notices that her back feels looser and her mood is a little lighter. Studies suggest that movement can help mood in modest ways, though everyone responds differently.
After moving, Mei sits in a chair and breathes slowly with her eyes closed. A few minutes of slow breathing can calm many people, and the research is promising even though it is mixed.
The method is very simple, and anyone can learn it in a minute. Breathe in gently through your nose for a count of four, then breathe out slowly for a count of six.
Mei puts one hand on her belly and feels it rise and fall with each breath. If she ever feels dizzy, she stops and breathes normally, because there is no prize for forcing it.
When her thoughts race around the room, Mei counts her breaths from one to ten. The numbers give a busy mind something simple to hold, and when she loses count she just starts again.
Some people prefer a square pattern: in for four, hold for four, out for four and hold for four. If holding your breath feels uncomfortable, simply leave out the holds.
People with asthma or other lung conditions should keep breathing exercises very gentle and ask a doctor if they are unsure. Slow breathing is meant to feel easy, never like hard work.
Elena has no quiet room, but she does have a kettle that takes two minutes to boil. She stands beside it, takes three slow breaths and watches the steam rise while Mateo plays.
One morning Elena invites Mateo to breathe like a balloon, filling up slowly and then letting the air out. He giggles, copies her and, for a few seconds, both of them are perfectly still.
After ten days, Mei notices that she uses the same slow breaths at work. Before she opens a difficult email, she pauses for a moment and lets her shoulders drop.
Breathing can be a two-minute part of your first hour, and no more than that. If you find that you do not enjoy it, you can drop it and try the next idea.
Now we come to the quietest part of the whole hour, which is the silence. Mei sits by the window for five minutes with no phone, no music and no book, and simply lets herself be still.
Meditation sounds mysterious, but at its simplest it means paying attention to one thing on purpose. That one thing can be your breath, a sound in the room or the feeling of your feet on the floor.
At first Mei's mind is crowded with thoughts about work, dinner and the thing she said last week. When she notices that she has drifted away, she gently brings her attention back to her breath.
Many beginners believe that meditation means having an empty mind, and they decide they are bad at it. But everyone's mind wanders, and a busy head is just the ordinary place where you begin.
On her first try, Mei is restless and checks the clock four times in five minutes. Then she hears the soft hum of the fridge, a sound she has heard every day and never noticed.
Studies suggest that meditation can modestly reduce stress and worry in some people. It is not a cure for any illness, and scientists are still working out who benefits most.
You do not have to meditate to enjoy a few quiet minutes. You can drink tea slowly, listen to the rain, say a prayer if you pray or simply look out of the window.
To stop herself checking the clock, Mei sets a soft timer for two minutes. When two minutes feels easy, she adds one more, and she builds up slowly over the weeks.
Mei always sits in the same chair in the same quiet corner of the living room. The place itself becomes a signal, and her mind begins to settle as soon as she sits down.
One afternoon a colleague speaks to Mei in a sharp voice. She feels the old anger rise, but she waits for one breath before answering, and her reply comes out calm and clear.
At the kitchen table, Mei opens her notebook and writes three short lines. Each line names something she is grateful for, and each one takes only a few seconds.

Studies suggest that writing about gratitude can lift mood a little for some people, though the effect is modest. Specific details seem to work better, so Mei writes about a particular moment rather than about her life in general.
On Tuesday Mei writes that her neighbour carried her bins in, that her shower was properly hot and that Dana told a joke at lunch. These are tiny things, and they make her smile.
Gratitude does not mean pretending that everything is fine. On a bad day Mei writes just one small true thing, such as the taste of toast, and that is enough.
After the thankful lines, Mei writes freely for a few minutes about whatever is on her mind. Her pen moves quickly, and she does not stop to fix anything.
This writing is only for you, so you can ignore spelling, grammar and style. Keep your pen moving, and if the subject becomes too painful, stop and speak to someone you trust.

Putting worries onto paper can make them feel smaller and clearer, as if you had moved them out of your head. Research on this kind of writing shows modest benefits, and it seems to help some people more than others.
Mei prefers a paper notebook because paper never sends her notifications or tempts her to check the news. Any tool that you will actually use is fine, though, so choose what works for you.
After two weeks, Mei sits down and reads her old pages from the beginning. She sees the same worries returning, but she also sees that many of them have already gone away.
Elena does not have time for three lines and a page of free writing. She writes just one line each morning, usually about something funny that Mateo did the day before.
Mei reads a few pages of a book that teaches her something or lifts her spirits. Ten pages a day add up to several books a year.
Choose a book that you actually want to read, and not one that you think you should. Mei leaves hers on her chair every night, so it is waiting for her in the morning.
If ten pages feels like too many, begin with two. Reading a little every day beats reading a lot now and then, because the habit builds the pile of finished books.
Not everyone enjoys reading print early in the morning, and that is perfectly fine. Listening to a book while you walk or tidy up the kitchen counts as feeding your mind too.
Next Mei spends ten minutes learning something that is new to her. She has always wanted to speak Spanish, so she writes five new words in her notebook and says each one aloud.
Before she learns new words, Mei reviews the ones from yesterday. Research on memory shows that coming back to something after a pause helps it stay in your mind for much longer.
The new thing does not have to be a language. It can be a guitar chord, a chess puzzle, a coding lesson or one new fact about the stars.
Mei has learned an important trick: she stops while the lesson is still interesting. If she leaves wanting a little more, she looks forward to returning tomorrow.
After three weeks, Mei has finished her first book, and she has learned about sixty new Spanish words. These numbers are not impressive on their own, but she had none of them before.
Reading and learning together take Mei about twenty minutes, although you can do either one in five. If your hour is short, you can skip this part, and the rest will still work.
Mei takes a plain card and writes her main goal on it in large letters. She wants to pass an important accounting exam in the spring, and she puts the card where she will see it.
A good goal is clear and specific, so it can be acted on. Instead of writing that she wants to do well, Mei writes her exam date and the hours she plans to study each week.

Small amounts of movement count for far more than we usually imagine, particularly when they are repeated every single day of the week.

The World Health Organization suggests that adults aim for at least one hundred and fifty minutes of moderate activity each week, spread across the days in whatever way suits them. That figure is a general guide and not a test you can fail, and any amount of movement is better than none. A few minutes each morning is a very good place to begin, and it is a better one than a heroic plan that you abandon by Friday.

On the fourth morning, Mei steps outside and walks for ten minutes along her quiet street, past closed shops and a man sweeping his doorstep. A short walk gives her daylight and movement in a single action, which feels like a bargain. She returns home with pink cheeks, a lighter step and, for once in her busy life, a mind that is pleasantly empty.

Mei does the sums on the back of an envelope and is quietly delighted. Ten minutes of walking every day for a week comes to seventy minutes, which is already nearly half of the weekly figure suggested by health experts. Nobody needed to buy a gym membership, travel across town or change into special clothes, and the whole thing cost her nothing at all.

How fast should you walk, jog or swim for the effort to count as moderate activity, and how will you know? A common rule of thumb says that moderate activity should leave you able to hold a conversation but unable to sing a whole song without gasping. It is a rough guide, and it has the great advantage of needing no equipment at all.

Health guidelines also suggest that adults work their muscles on at least two days a week, and so Mei begins very gently with five slow stands up from a chair. She counts each one aloud, breathes steadily and does not hurry, since slow and careful movements are safer for a beginner. After a fortnight she may try six, and after another fortnight perhaps seven, but there is no hurry and no one is counting.

If you have a heart problem, an injury, a long-term illness or a pregnancy, it is wise to speak to a doctor before you begin any new exercise. Everyone, in any case, should start slowly and build up over time, and no routine is worth hurting yourself for. This book gives general ideas that many people have found useful, and it is not a substitute for personal advice from a qualified professional.

By the end of the first week, Mei notices that her back feels looser and that her mood is a little lighter by the time she reaches the office. Studies suggest that regular movement can lift mood in modest ways, though everyone responds differently and no single walk will cure a bad week. It is enough, for now, that she looks forward to the next one with something close to pleasure, which is rare for a person of her habits.

After her stretches, Mei sits in a chair, closes her eyes and breathes slowly for a few minutes. Slow breathing can calm many people, and the research on it is promising, although the results are mixed and the effects tend to be modest. It costs nothing, takes no skill and can be tried by anyone sitting down.

The method could hardly be simpler, and anyone who can sit in a chair can begin it today. Breathe in gently through the nose for a count of four, then let the breath out slowly through the mouth for a count of six, and repeat that for two or three minutes. The longer out-breath is what gives the exercise its soothing reputation, though the exact numbers are not sacred.

Mei rests one hand on her belly and feels it rise and fall with each breath, which gives her mind something definite to follow. If she ever feels dizzy or uncomfortable, she stops and breathes normally again, since there is no prize for forcing the exercise. Gentle is the only setting that works for this kind of exercise, and anything more forceful defeats its purpose before it has begun.

When her thoughts begin racing around the room like startled birds, Mei counts her breaths from one to ten and then begins again. The numbers give a busy mind something simple to hold, and when she loses count, which happens often, she merely starts over without fuss. Losing count is not a failure at all, because noticing that you have lost count and beginning again is exactly the exercise.

Some people prefer a square pattern, in which they breathe in for four counts, hold for four, breathe out for four and hold again for four. It suits those who like a clear structure, but if holding your breath feels uncomfortable, you can leave the pauses out entirely. The best pattern, in the end, is the one that you are willing and able to do again tomorrow morning without a fight.

People with asthma or other lung conditions should keep any breathing exercise very gentle, and they would be wise to ask a doctor if they are unsure. Slow breathing is supposed to feel easy and natural, and never like hard work or a contest. There is nothing to prove to anybody, so there is nothing to push against, and the whole exercise can be as soft as you like.

Elena has no quiet room and no spare half hour, but she does have a kettle that takes two minutes to boil. She stands beside it, takes three slow breaths with her eyes half closed and watches the steam curl upwards while Mateo bangs a wooden spoon on the floor. It is not a retreat, yet it is something, and something is a great deal more than nothing.

One morning Elena invites Mateo to breathe like a balloon, filling slowly with air and then letting it out with a long, floppy sigh. He giggles, copies her and for a few precious seconds the whole room goes still. Neither of them could say exactly what happened, but both of them feel a little lighter afterwards.

After ten days, Mei notices that she has begun to use the same slow breaths in the middle of her working day. Before she opens a difficult email or walks into a tense meeting, she pauses for a moment, lets her shoulders drop and breathes out for longer than she breathes in. The habit that began in the quiet of the morning has quietly started to travel with her into the busiest hours of the day.

Breathing can be a two-minute part of your first hour, and it does not need to be any longer than that. If you try it for a week and find that it does nothing for you, you may drop it without a trace of guilt and move on to the next idea. The only wrong choice is to carry on with something that makes the morning worse.

Now we arrive at the quietest part of the whole hour, the part that most people find the hardest. Mei sits cross-legged by the window for five minutes with no phone, no music and no book, and simply lets herself be still. After so many years of filling every gap with noise, the silence feels strange, and then slowly it begins to feel like a gift.

Meditation sounds mysterious, but at its simplest it means paying attention to one thing on purpose and noticing when your mind has wandered away from it. That one thing can be the breath, a sound in the room or the feeling of your feet on the floor. It is a very old practice, and it is practised in many forms all over the world.

At first Mei's mind is crowded with thoughts about work, about dinner and about something embarrassing she said last week. Each time she notices that she has drifted away, she gently brings her attention back to the breath, without scolding herself for wandering. The noticing, she learns, is not a distraction from the practice; it is the practice.

Many beginners believe that meditation requires a perfectly empty mind, and they conclude from the first minute that they are hopeless at it. In truth everybody's mind wanders, including that of people who have practised for decades, and a busy head is simply the ordinary place where you begin. The goal is not a blank; it is a gentler relationship with the noise.

On her first try Mei is restless, fidgets twice and checks the clock four times in five minutes. Then she begins to hear the soft hum of the refrigerator, a sound that has been there every day of her life and which she has never really noticed. For a moment her whole attention rests there, and the restlessness that was tugging at her all through the previous minutes quietly loosens its grip.

A number of studies suggest that meditation can modestly reduce stress and anxiety in some people, though the results vary and some of the research is of poor quality. It is not a cure for any illness, and scientists are still working out who benefits most and why. Treat it as a pleasant and sometimes useful tool for the mind, and not as a miracle that will solve everything for you.

You do not have to call it meditation to enjoy a few quiet minutes. You might drink a cup of tea slowly, listen to rain on the glass, say a prayer if you are a person of faith or simply sit and look out of the window. What matters is that for a short time nothing is being asked of you.

To stop herself from checking the clock, Mei sets a gentle timer for two minutes and puts it out of sight. When two minutes begins to feel easy she adds one more, and over several weeks she builds slowly towards ten. Growing by a minute at a time is almost too small to notice, which is exactly how it works.

Mei always sits in the same chair in the same quiet corner of the living room, with the same blanket over her knees. The place itself becomes a signal, and her mind begins to settle almost as soon as she sits down, in the way that a dog circles before it lies down. A familiar corner, kept for this purpose alone, can do much of the work of calming you down without any help from your willpower.

One afternoon a colleague speaks to Mei in a sharp and impatient voice, and she feels the old anger rise in her chest. She waits for a single breath before she replies, and the answer that emerges is calm, clear and entirely free of regret. That tiny gap between feeling and reacting is, she suspects, the most valuable thing the quiet minutes have given her.

At the kitchen table Mei opens her green notebook and writes three short lines, each of them naming something she is grateful for. None of the lines takes more than a few seconds, and none of them has to be impressive or profound. The idea is simply to point her attention at what is going well, which it rarely does by itself.

Studies suggest that writing about gratitude can lift mood a little for some people, although the effect is modest and not everyone benefits. Specific details seem to work better than grand statements, so Mei writes about one particular moment instead of announcing that she is grateful for her life. A sentence about the warm bread is worth more than a paragraph about happiness.

On Tuesday Mei writes that her neighbour carried the bins back in for her, that her shower was properly hot for the first time in a week and that Dana told a joke at lunch which was truly funny. They are tiny things, nothing that anybody would put on a list of achievements, and she would never have remembered them by evening. On the page they gather quietly together into what looks, to her surprise, like a rather good day that she had almost missed.

Gratitude does not mean pretending that everything is fine or that problems are not real. On a bad day Mei writes just one small true thing, such as the taste of toast or the warmth of a scarf, and she lets the rest of the page stay empty. Forced cheerfulness helps no one, whereas an honest pen, even when it writes something small and plain, is always better than a false smile.

After the grateful lines, Mei writes freely for a few minutes about whatever happens to be on her mind: a worry, a plan, a half-formed idea. Her pen moves quickly across the page, and she does not stop to correct a single word. Thoughts that seemed tangled in her head become oddly simple once she can see them.

This writing is for your eyes alone, so you can ignore spelling, grammar and style entirely and let the pen run on. If a subject turns out to be too painful, you are free to stop, and it would be wise to talk to a friend, a doctor or a counsellor about it. A notebook is a good listener, but it is not a substitute for people.

Putting worries onto paper can make them feel smaller and clearer, as though you had moved them out of your head and onto a shelf. Research on this kind of writing has found modest benefits, and it appears to help some people far more than it helps others. If it feels like a relief to you, that is reason enough to keep going.

Mei prefers a paper notebook because paper never lights up with notifications and never tempts her to check the news halfway through a sentence. That is a personal choice, and any tool that you will actually use every day is perfectly fine, whether it is a diary, a typed file or a voice note. The best system, in the end, is the one that survives the second week, and then the third, and then the busy months that follow.

After two weeks, Mei sits down with a cup of tea and reads her old pages from the very beginning. She sees certain worries returning again and again, and she sees something even more interesting: most of the things that seemed enormous on page three have quietly disappeared. Her own handwriting, tilted and hurried as it is, turns out to be rather good at the delicate business of reassurance.

Elena has no time for three grateful lines and a page of free writing, so she keeps her version tiny. She writes one line each morning on a sticky note, usually about something funny or sweet that Mateo did the day before. A small habit that is kept is worth more than a large one that exists only in good intentions.

Mei reads a few pages of a book that teaches her something new or lifts her spirits, before the demands of the day can interrupt. Ten pages a day come to more than three thousand pages in a year, which is roughly the length of ten ordinary novels. Reading, she says, is the only part of her morning in which time seems to move at an easy pace.

Choose a book that you truly want to read and not one that you feel you ought to, because duty is a poor companion at six in the morning. Mei leaves hers on the armchair each evening, bookmarked at the right page, so that it waits for her like a patient companion. Placing the right object exactly where your eyes will fall on it does half of the work.

If ten pages sounds like too many for a busy morning, begin with two and let the habit grow on its own schedule. Reading a little every day is better than reading a great deal now and then, since it is the steady rhythm that builds a long list of finished books. A page is a very small thing, but pages are what books are made of.

Not everyone enjoys reading print in the early morning, and many people find that their eyes are tired before the day has even begun. Listening to a book while you walk, or while you tidy the kitchen, can feed the mind just as well and fits neatly into the rest of the hour. The format matters far less than the habit of letting good ideas in at a time of day when the mind is open.

Next Mei spends ten minutes learning something that has nothing to do with her job. She has always dreamed of speaking Spanish, so she writes five new words in her notebook, says each one aloud and tries to make a short sentence from them. The sentences are clumsy and she makes at least three mistakes, but they belong to her and that is exactly why she enjoys them.

Before she learns any new words, Mei reviews the ones from yesterday and the day before. Research on memory has shown repeatedly that returning to a fact after a short pause helps it stay in the mind for far longer than studying it once in a long session. Little and often turns out to be not only the gentler way to learn but also, quite possibly, the cleverer one.

The new thing does not have to be a language, and it does not have to be useful. It can be a guitar chord, a chess puzzle, a lesson in coding, a drawing technique or a single astonishing fact about the stars. Curiosity is a muscle, and it grows stronger whenever it is allowed to follow its own nose.

Mei has discovered an important trick, which is to stop while the lesson is still interesting rather than when she has squeezed every drop from it. If she leaves wanting a little more, she looks forward to returning the next morning, and the habit sustains itself on that appetite. Nobody has ever stuck with something for long once it began to feel like homework, so it is wise to keep the pleasure alive.

After three weeks, Mei has finished her first book and has learned about sixty new Spanish words, and she can say a few simple sentences to a surprised barista. These numbers are not remarkable on their own, but a month earlier she had no part of them. Ten quiet minutes, repeated day after day without fuss, have built something that she can see, count and be rightly proud of.

Reading and learning together take Mei about twenty minutes, though you can do either of them in five and a few people can manage neither. If your hour is short, this is the first part that you may happily skip, and the rest of the routine will still do its work. A morning that is not crowded is a morning that you are more likely to repeat.

Mei takes a plain white card and writes her main goal across it in large letters. She wants to pass an important professional exam in the spring, a goal that has been drifting in the back of her mind for two years without ever becoming real. Seeing it on a card, in her own handwriting, makes it feel like a promise rather than a wish.

A good goal is clear and specific, and a vague one is almost impossible to act on. Instead of writing that she wants to do well in her career, Mei writes the date of the exam and the number of hours she plans to study each week. You can only walk towards something that you can point to, and a vague wish gives you nothing to point at.

Every morning Mei props the card against her notebook and reads it once, slowly, before she does anything else. It takes only five seconds, but it reminds her what the early effort is for and which direction she has decided to face. Without that reminder a good routine can turn into a pleasant habit that goes nowhere.

Next Mei writes down the three most important tasks of the day on a small yellow note. She does not attempt to list everything, only the three things that would make the day feel worthwhile if they were finished, and she resists the urge to add a fourth. A short list is a promise that can be kept, while a long one is only a source of worry.

One of the three tasks is always more important than the others, and Mei circles it in a thick pen. She tries to do that one first, while her mind is fresh and before the small jobs and the interruptions have a chance to gather. The rest of the list can then be dealt with, but the day has already been won.

Mei closes her eyes for a minute and imagines how the day ahead is likely to unfold. She pictures the steps she will take, one after another, and not only the happy result waiting at the end. Some research suggests that rehearsing the process helps people more than daydreaming about success.

She has a difficult meeting at two o'clock, so she pictures it in some detail, from the walk down the corridor to the first sentence she will speak. She imagines what she will say if somebody interrupts her, and how she will breathe and keep her voice steady. When the moment arrives, it feels oddly familiar, as if she has been there before.

Research on what psychologists call implementation plans suggests that statements of the form “when this happens, I will do that” help people follow through on their intentions. Mei writes, “At half past seven I sit down at the table and study for twenty minutes,” and she is surprised how much easier the decision feels. A plan with a time and a place leaves very little room for arguments.

Mei also takes a realistic look at what might go wrong, because a hopeful plan with no obstacles in it is only a daydream. If she feels too tired to study, she decides, she will read one page of her textbook and nothing more. Planning for trouble in advance keeps small problems from growing into convenient excuses, because the answer is already waiting on the card.

One morning Mei sees that her list has crept up to six items, and she realises she has let it become a burden again. She crosses off the three least important tasks, tells a colleague that one of them can wait until Friday and discovers that nothing bad follows. Saying no, she finds, is not rude when it protects the things that matter most.

Now comes the part that makes the rest worthwhile: Mei takes one small step on something that truly matters to her. She opens her exam textbook and studies a single topic for twenty minutes, before the office, the emails and the telephone have had a chance to claim her. It is not a lot, but it is a start, and a start is the hardest thing.

For many people the mind is at its freshest and quietest early in the day, before the demands of other people arrive in a flood. Mei finds that twenty minutes of study at this hour are worth far more than an hour in the tired evening, although this will not be true for everybody. Learn when your own best attention happens to arrive, and guard that precious time as carefully as you would guard a valuable appointment.

If the task feels too large to face, shrink the first step until it is almost laughable. Open the file, write a single sentence or read one page, and you will often find that the momentum carries you further than you planned. Beginning is the heavy part of any task, while continuing is usually much lighter once the first few minutes have passed.

Mei leaves her laptop closed until her own small piece of work is done, and she drinks her tea in peace. If she opened her email first, other people's priorities would jump to the front of the queue, and hers would be pushed quietly to the back. Email is useful, but it is a list of what others want from you, and it can wait twenty minutes.

While she studies, Mei puts her phone in a drawer and works on one thing only. Research has shown repeatedly that switching between tasks costs time and attention, and that people who believe they are good at it are often fooling themselves. Doing one thing at a time may feel old-fashioned in a world of constant pings, but it works better than almost anything else.

Mei sets a timer for twenty minutes and promises herself that she will work until it rings and no longer. Knowing that the end is near makes it far easier to begin, and when the bell goes she takes a short break to stretch and look at the sky. A clear boundary of this kind is one of the oldest and most reliable tricks for beating the natural reluctance to begin.

Some mornings Mei feels stuck before she has even begun, and the hardest chapter of the book glares up at her from the page. On those mornings she starts with the easiest section instead, because a small success gives her the confidence to tackle the harder part afterwards. Momentum, like a snowball rolling down a gentle hill, grows steadily as it moves, and the first small push is all it needs.

Dana's own small step looks nothing like Mei's, and that is how it should be. Each morning she writes one page of a children's story for her young niece, and after seven weeks she is already halfway through a book that she once thought she would never begin. The step belongs to you, and so does the direction, and nobody else can decide for you what is worth your first twenty minutes.

Dana's first pages are rough, and several of them are frankly dreadful, but she keeps them anyway and moves on. A rough page can be improved on another day, whereas a blank page can only be stared at. Waiting to be perfect before you start is just a polite way of not starting, and it fools almost everybody at least once.

After thirty days of twenty-minute sessions, Mei has studied for about ten hours before most people have finished their breakfast. She did not sacrifice any evenings or weekends to do it, and her exam, which once loomed like a mountain, now looks like a hill with a path up it. Small steps do not feel like much while you are taking them, which is exactly why so many people give up before they add up.

At last Mei sits down to a proper breakfast, and for the first time in years she eats it slowly and with attention. She tastes the bread, notices the sharpness of the jam and realises that she has been swallowing her mornings whole. A meal eaten without hurry is a small holiday that costs nothing extra, and it can be taken every single morning of the year.

This book is not a diet, and it has no list of forbidden foods, because the right breakfast varies enormously from one person to the next. Eat what you enjoy and what makes you feel well, and if you are simply not hungry early in the morning, that is perfectly acceptable. Anyone who lives with a medical condition should follow the advice of their own doctor and treat these ideas as general information only.

Mei eats without a screen in front of her, and she begins to notice the taste, the warmth and the texture of the food. A few studies suggest that giving a meal your full attention makes it more satisfying, although the evidence is modest and nobody should expect miracles from a piece of toast. At the very least, the toast tastes better when you are paying attention to it, and that alone is a modest reward.

Mei remembers that a routine which feels like a chore will not last, so one morning she turns on some lively music and dances around her kitchen with a wooden spoon. She feels thoroughly ridiculous for about ten seconds, and then, quite suddenly, she feels wonderful. Enjoyment is not a reward for the hard part; it is part of the method.

Mei makes a short list of three songs that have never failed to lift her mood, and she plays them in the same order while she gets ready. Before long, the first few notes act as a signal, and her body begins to wake up and sway before her mind has caught up. Music has a way of reaching places in the mind where instructions and good intentions can never go, and it does so without a sound of complaint.

Mei decides to turn the hour into a small treat instead of a duty, and she begins to surround it with things she loves. She buys a mug that feels right in her hands, keeps a soft blanket on her chair and lights a small candle on the table. Anything that makes you want to come back to the habit the next day is a perfectly good tool, however trivial it may look.

On her small balcony Mei waters a row of pots and breathes the cool morning air while the city slowly wakes up below. Many people say that time among green things leaves them calm, and some studies support this, although a plant is hardly a medical treatment. She enjoys the leaves for their own sake, without expecting anything from them, and that is reason enough to keep watering them each morning.

One morning Mei looks up in the middle of a rather enthusiastic dance and sees her neighbour watching from the opposite window. For a second she is mortified, and then both of them burst out laughing, and the neighbour raises a thumb in approval. It turns out that nobody minds being seen enjoying their own morning, and some people are even encouraged to try the same thing.

After a whole week of early mornings, Mei marks the occasion with a modest celebration on Friday. She buys two pastries on her way to work, one for herself and one for Dana, who first suggested the notebook. Rewarding effort is not self-indulgence; it tells the mind that effort is something worth repeating.

Mei notices that her mornings now hold pleasure as well as discipline, and that it is the pleasure which brings her back day after day. A routine that is only a duty is likely to collapse at the first sign of stress, whereas one that feels like a gift can survive almost anything. She stops thinking of it as a regime and begins to think of it as a habit of kindness.

You do not have to do everything described in this book, and Mei certainly does not do all of it on any single morning. Choose the three or four parts that suit your life, and be ready to drop anything that does not suit you. A routine that truly fits you will always beat one that merely impresses other people.

If you are a beginner, begin with just ten minutes, and resist the temptation to build a grand routine on the very first day. When ten minutes feels easy, add a few more, and let the hour expand only if you truly want it to. Ambition is welcome here, but it should learn to walk before it runs, and a patient beginning makes for a longer journey.

Here is a sample menu for a tight ten minutes: a glass of water, a pause at the window for daylight, a gentle stretch and three lines in a notebook. It is modest enough to survive a bad night, yet it contains a little of everything that matters in this book. Many people never need more than that for years at a time, and some of them find that ten minutes is exactly right for them.

Doing your routine at roughly the same time each day makes it feel increasingly automatic, as the hour itself becomes the cue. After a while you stop asking yourself whether you will do it today, and the question quietly disappears. The less you have to decide, the more energy you have left for the thing itself.

Mei links her new habit to something she already does without thinking every day. She puts her notebook next to the kettle, so that the act of making tea reminds her to sit and write. Attaching a new habit to an old one is a bit like hanging a new picture on an existing nail.

How long does it take to form a habit that feels automatic, and what do we really know about it? One well-known study of volunteers found that it took about two months on average, although the range was enormous, from a few weeks to the better part of a year. The old claim that twenty-one days is enough is a myth, and you need not feel ashamed if you are slower than that.

A habit is far easier to keep when the first step is easy, so make the first step as smooth as you can. Leave the mat unrolled, the book on the chair and your shoes by the door, and remove anything that stands between you and the beginning. Willpower is wildly overrated as a tool, whereas a well-arranged room does much of the work for you without any argument at all.

If you want to add something new, take something else away, or the hour will swell until it becomes a source of stress. A routine that keeps growing is a routine that is on its way to being abandoned, and the point was always to feel calmer. Treat the time you have as a small suitcase, and pack it carefully, since there is no room in it for anything you do not need.

Online you will find endless photographs of perfect mornings, complete with green juice, sunrise yoga and spotless kitchens. They show the best minute of somebody's day, carefully arranged for an audience, and they tell you nothing about your own life. Your routine is not a performance for an audience, and nobody is giving out marks, so you are free to make it as plain as you like.

By the third week, Mei has chosen the five parts that she likes best: daylight, water, a short walk, three lines of gratitude and twenty minutes of study. The whole routine takes about forty minutes, and every part of it is there because she wanted it to be. She has not copied anybody's perfect morning from a photograph; she has patiently built her own, one small and honest piece at a time.

In the fourth week, to her dismay, everything seems to go wrong at once and without any warning. Mei sleeps badly for three nights in a row, the rain hammers on the window and she lies in bed wondering why she ever thought that a notebook could change anything. The early enthusiasm of the first weeks has completely gone, and only the plain habit is left, which is precisely when a habit is tested.

The end of the quarter has arrived, and the accounts on Mei's desk are piling up like snow. She stays late at the office night after night, reaches home after nine and falls into bed at midnight, with her head still running through columns of figures. Under that kind of pressure, even the best and most carefully planned routine has to bend a little if it is to survive at all.

A voice in Mei's head insists that this is pointless, that she was never a routine person and that she should give up before she embarrasses herself. She notices the voice, as she has learned to notice her wandering thoughts in the quiet minutes, and she does not let it make the decision. Thoughts are like the weather passing across the sky, and they are not instructions that she is obliged to follow.

On the tired mornings, Mei does a shortened version of her routine, and she does it without an ounce of guilt. She drinks her water, stands at the window for a minute, writes a single line in her notebook and then gets on with the day. It is not impressive to look at, but it keeps the thread of the habit unbroken until the pressure of the week has eased.

Mei writes a card for her hardest days, and it has only three steps on it: water, window and one line. When she is exhausted she does not have to decide anything or negotiate with herself, because she can simply obey the card. A plan made by your rested self is a gift to your tired self.

One grey morning Mei sleeps straight through her alarm and misses the entire routine, from the water to the notebook. She does not scold herself or announce that everything is ruined, and the next morning she simply picks up her notebook where she left it. A single missed day is a small bump, and it does not wipe out what you have done.

Many people think, “I missed one day, so I have failed and I might as well stop,” and that all-or-nothing thinking has ended more good habits than any busy schedule ever did. A calendar with one gap in it is still a calendar full of effort. Judge the pattern over a month, and not the result of a single morning.

If you are badly short of sleep, the wisest choice may be to rest a little longer and begin the hour later or in a smaller form. A routine exists to serve you, and you do not exist to serve it, so listen to what your body is telling you. Pushing through exhaustion every day is not discipline; it is a different kind of mistake.

Mei catches a heavy cold and spends three days wrapped in a blanket with tea, tissues and very little ambition. When you are ill, the routine is not important, because rest is the thing your body needs, and the routine will still be there when you are well again. On the fourth day she returns with only a cup of tea, and that is plenty.

Mei learns that a routine which bends will outlast one that is stiff and strict, much as a reed survives a storm that breaks an oak. By the end of that hard month she is prouder of her shortened mornings than of her best ones, because they were the ones that took real courage. The hour is not a test of perfection; it is a place to come back to.

Kofi sits in his kitchen with a cup of tea while the afternoon sun slants across the table, and for him this is the morning. Shift workers can use the first hour after they wake, whenever that happens to be, and the idea works just as well at four o'clock as it does at six. The clock on the wall matters much less than the choice you make about how to spend the first hour after waking.

Kofi's shift runs from seven in the evening until seven in the morning, through the darkest hours that most people spend asleep. He checks on patients, prepares medicines and answers calls, and although the ward is quieter than during the day, it never truly falls silent. By the end of the shift his body is crying out for rest, and he has been awake through the whole of the night.

When his shift ends, Kofi walks home as the sun is rising and wears a pair of dark glasses against the glare. Some night workers find that avoiding bright morning light on the journey home helps their bodies treat the coming sleep as night, though people differ and the evidence is mixed. He is not trying to be mysterious or dramatic with these precautions; he is simply trying to give himself the chance to rest properly.

Sleeping in the daytime is difficult, because the world is bright and noisy, so Kofi protects his rest with great care. He has thick dark curtains, a pair of earplugs, a sign on the door and a phone that stays silent until he wakes. The first hour of his day has to be earned by the last hour of his sleep.

Kofi explains his sleeping hours to his family and to his neighbours, so that they know exactly when to keep the noise down and when it is safe to knock. Most people are only too glad to help once they understand, and a little explanation saves a great deal of silent resentment. Asking for what you need is not selfish; it is how a plan becomes real.

When Kofi wakes, he opens the curtains, drinks a tall glass of water and stands on the balcony in whatever daylight is left. He stretches for five minutes, reads ten pages of a novel and writes three lines of thanks, all before he thinks about the ward. It is exactly the same hour as Mei's, only wearing a different coat, and it begins when the sun is about to set.

His colleague Joy laughs out loud when Kofi describes his first hour, and says that nurses have no time for such luxuries. A week later she joins him for a cup of tea before their shift begins, sits in silence for five minutes and admits, with some surprise, that it is rather nice. Habits spread more easily through friendship and example than through advice, and Joy has just become a very good example of it.

Working through the night can be hard on sleep and health over many years, because it asks the body to do the opposite of what it naturally wants. Researchers are still studying how great the risks are and who is most affected, and anyone who struggles should talk to a doctor or a workplace health service. A good morning routine can help, but it is not a cure for a difficult schedule.

Kofi packs a proper meal and some fruit to take to work, and he drinks his coffee only in the first half of the shift. Many night workers find that caffeine late in the shift makes daytime sleep much harder, though the effect varies widely from one person to another. He has learned to plan the end of his night from the beginning, because the choices he makes at midnight decide how he sleeps at eight.

On his days off, Kofi must choose between staying on his night schedule and joining the rest of his family in the daytime. He moves his sleep partway towards theirs, never all the way, and he keeps the first hour of his day at much the same time as before. A compromise is not a failure; it is how real people manage real lives.

Elena begins her first hour at the moment Mateo wakes up, and she makes no attempt to hide from him. She stretches in the living room with her arms above her head, and he copies every movement, collapsing into giggles when she topples sideways. A parent's routine may need to be short and noisy, but it can still be real.

Each morning Elena carries Mateo to the window, where together they pull open the curtains and say good morning to the sun and the pigeons. The daylight helps her own body clock, and the little ritual gives her son a cheerful beginning to the day that he will not remember but will still absorb. Two small people can share one small habit, and each of them will remember it in a different and entirely private way.

Many guides tell parents to wake before their children and seize a quiet hour, but Elena disagrees with this advice. When she has had a broken night, sleep matters far more than any routine, and she allows herself to stay in bed until the last possible moment. A rested parent who skips the notebook beats an exhausted one who does everything on the list.

Elena's husband Omar leaves early for work on weekdays, but on Saturdays he takes charge of Mateo and builds towers of blocks on the living room floor. That gives Elena twenty minutes entirely to herself, and she spends them with tea, silence and a notebook. Sharing the load is not a luxury; for many families it is the only way a routine becomes possible.

If you are naturally an evening person, there is little point in forcing yourself out of bed at five in the morning and then spending the hour yawning. A first hour that begins at nine, when your mind is ready and willing, is far better than a miserable one that begins in the dark. Your body clock is not an enemy to be defeated, but a rather stubborn companion that is much better to cooperate with than to fight.

Some owls have jobs that start early, and for them an adjustment may be unavoidable. Move your wake time earlier by about fifteen minutes every few days instead of an hour in one jump, and get as much morning light as you can on the way. Gentle changes are far more likely to last than sudden ones, since the body, like a ship, turns best when it turns slowly.

On Saturdays and Sundays Mei uses a gentler version of her hour, which she calls her slow morning. She still drinks her tea and reads a few pages of a book, but she keeps the alarm off and lets the day begin when she is ready. Even so, she tries not to drift more than an hour from her usual waking time.

When Mei travels for work, she packs her small green notebook and a pen at the top of her bag. In a strange hotel room, with traffic outside and an unfamiliar bed, the same few quiet minutes make her feel at home. Light from a new window can also help the body clock adjust to a different time zone, although recovery is gradual.

If you live in a small or shared home, you may not have a private room to call your own. Find a quiet corner, wear headphones or earplugs, or even sit on the edge of the bath for your five quiet minutes, with the door politely closed. The setting matters much less than the intention behind it, and a bathroom floor can be as peaceful as a mountain top.

At the end of the month Elena counts the ticks on her calendar and finds that she did something on four days out of every seven. She is delighted, because for a mother of a two-year-old, four is a triumph, and four is an enormous amount more than none. Success, in a real life with real children, has never meant perfection, and it never will, however many guides suggest otherwise.

A morning routine is not a cure for anything, and it was never meant to be one. If you feel low or anxious for a long time, it is wise to talk to a doctor, and there is no shame whatsoever in doing so. Looking for help is a sign of good sense, in the same way that visiting a dentist is.

If low mood, constant worry or very poor sleep lasts for more than a couple of weeks, please speak to a doctor or another health professional. If you ever have thoughts of harming yourself, contact the emergency services or a crisis line in your country at once, and do not wait. No notebook, no matter how green or how lovingly kept, is a replacement for the help of another person who is trained to listen.

If you feel heavily sleepy all day despite a full night in bed, or if you have been told that you snore loudly and sometimes stop breathing, mention it to a doctor. Some sleep problems have medical causes that no amount of lamp-dimming can fix, and they are often very treatable once they are recognised. Tiredness is a signal from the body, and sometimes it points to something more serious than a weak habit or a poor bedtime.

A morning routine cannot repair a job that demands too much, money worries that keep you awake or heavy duties of caring for others. For problems of that size you may need practical help, a frank conversation or a change in the situation itself, and no amount of self-improvement can replace them. The hour can steady you and make you stronger, but it cannot do the whole job alone, and it was never meant to.

This book is general information, and it is not medical advice of any kind. It cannot know your body, your history or your medicines, and so you should ask a qualified professional about anything that concerns you personally. What you read here is meant to start a conversation with yourself, not to replace one with your doctor.

Be wary of anyone who promises to transform your whole life in thirty days, because real change is slow, uneven and rarely as dramatic as an advertisement. People who sell miracles are usually selling something else, and the evidence for a modest routine is, in the end, modest. That honesty is the only real reason that you should trust this book, and it applies to every idea in these pages.

Rising early does not make anyone a better person, and night owls are not lazy simply because their bodies run on a later clock. What matters is that you use your waking hours in a way that you are proud of, and that you treat your own rhythms with respect instead of embarrassment. Virtue has never depended on the hour at which a person happens to rise, and nobody who sleeps late should be made to feel ashamed.

You will read that famous and successful people all get up at five in the morning, and the claim is repeated so often that it begins to sound like a law. Those stories are anecdotes, however, and nobody counts the successful people who sleep late, nor the early risers who never achieve anything. A good habit has to prove itself in your own life, over your own weeks, and not in a magazine that is trying to sell you something.

The phone is not an enemy, and this book has no quarrel with technology, which brings us news, friends and a great deal of help. It is simply a question of who chooses the timing, so check your phone after your first hour, and do it on purpose and with open eyes. A tool you use deliberately is quite different from a habit that uses you.

When Mei's father goes into hospital for a week, her routine shrinks to five minutes at the kitchen table before the early bus. Even so, the water, the window and the stillness help her to feel steady, and they remind her that some part of the day still belongs to her. A small routine is most valuable when life is least predictable, because it gives you one fixed point while everything else moves around it.

Mei hangs a calendar on the kitchen wall and draws a green tick on every day that she does her hour, however short it happened to be. Within a few weeks the ticks form a satisfying chain, and she finds that she does not want to be the one to break it. Few things motivate quite like a little bit of visible evidence, and a row of green ticks is evidence that nobody can argue with.

Tracking should encourage you and never scold you, because a calendar is a mirror and not a judge. A missing tick is only information, and it tells you something about the shape of your week without saying anything at all about your worth. If the chart ever makes you anxious instead of proud, put it away for a while and return to it when you feel ready.

Mei and Dana meet for coffee on Saturday morning and compare their notebooks, laughing at each other's handwriting. Having a friend who is attempting the same thing makes both of them feel less alone and a good deal more determined. Telling another person about a plan makes it more real, and being asked about it later makes it harder to forget.

Each morning, as soon as her hour is finished, Mei sends Dana a single word and a smiling face, and she usually gets one back before she has put on her shoes. It takes five seconds and costs nothing, yet it gives each of them a small, warm sense of being accompanied. Encouragement is cheap to give and priceless to receive, and the two friends have discovered that it also grows when it is shared.

In the sixth week it is Dana's turn to struggle, and she confesses over lunch that she has missed five days and feels like a fraud. Mei does not give a lecture or a list of rules; she simply listens, laughs kindly at the idea of being a fraud and promises to message her tomorrow. Sometimes the best advice a person can offer is simply company, along with the quiet promise to be there again tomorrow.

After two weeks, Mei sits down with her notebook and her tea to review the experiment honestly. She looks at what has helped, what has felt like a burden and what she has simply done out of habit, and she decides to keep the good parts and drop the rest. A routine that is never reviewed slowly becomes a routine that no longer fits.

Mei asks herself four plain questions and writes her answers underneath each one, in her very best handwriting. What did I enjoy, what did I skip, what actually made me feel better and what would I like to change? Honest answers matter more than impressive ones, since nobody will ever mark them but her.

Mei notices that she never quite enjoys the free writing in the morning, whereas she loves it at night with a mug of something warm. So she moves it to the evening and uses the saved ten minutes to walk a little further in the morning sun. Changing a routine because it works better for you is not weakness, but wisdom.

A colleague asks why Mei seems so calm these days, and she answers lightly, without a trace of preaching. She explains what she does, what she has dropped and what she has learned, and she does not suggest that anyone else should copy her routine. People are rarely persuaded by lectures, but they are often curious about a friend who is happy.

Each evening Mei gives her day a score between one and ten and writes it in the corner of the calendar square, without much ceremony. After a month she studies the pattern and ignores the odd good or bad day, because the trend tells a truer story than any single number. It is not a scientific measurement of anything, but it is her own honest record, and she finds that it tells her plenty.

After a month of early mornings, Mei finishes an important report a full day early and leaves the office on time for the first time in ages. She is not a different person, and her job has not changed at all, but she feels calmer and more in charge of her days. The difference lives mostly in the way she begins her days, and she is beginning to suspect that this is where most differences live.

After a month Kofi is sleeping a little better, and he arrives at the ward feeling more awake and more patient with his patients. Difficult nights still happen, because night work is what it is, and he accepts that fact without blaming himself or his routine. A modest improvement, honestly measured, is worth more than a promise of perfect rest.

After a month Elena's mornings are every bit as busy as before, and Mateo is every bit as loud, but the tiny ritual at the window has made them feel warmer. She does not have an hour to herself, and she probably will not for a few years, yet she has found three minutes that are truly hers. Three minutes, it turns out, can carry quite a lot when they are protected from the noise and given a purpose of their own.

Be realistic about what to expect, because a good morning routine is not a miracle. It tends to bring modest gains in calm, focus and mood, and the benefits show themselves slowly, like a plant growing on a windowsill. Treat anyone who promises you much more than that with a healthy dose of scepticism.

In the spring, Mei sits her professional exam and passes it, and she cries a little at the kitchen table. She is the first to say that the studying did the real work, and that the early hour merely made room for it, as a clear table makes room for a meal. Small steps, taken for long enough and with a little patience, do reach the top, even when the top is out of sight.

One morning Mei turns back to the first page of her green notebook, where months ago she wrote three plain words. Calm, time and choice are all still there on the paper, and she realises that she has been living a little closer to each of them every day since. She did not find them in a miracle; she found them in a habit.

Here, in short, is the whole hour: drink a glass of water, find some daylight, move your body and sit for a few quiet minutes. Then read a little, write a little, choose your three tasks and take one small step on something that matters. Take what suits you, shorten what is too long and leave the rest behind.

Take a clean page and write your own menu in your own words, because the routine that matters is yours and not Mei's. Choose the parts that suit you, decide when your first hour begins and give it a name that makes you smile. A plan that you have built yourself is far easier to love than one you were handed.

Be kind to yourself during the first weeks, because they are practice and not an examination. You will forget, you will oversleep, you will change your mind and you will occasionally feel ridiculous, and every bit of that belongs to the learning. A habit grows best in friendly soil, and kindness is the best fertiliser there is.

So tonight, before you go to bed, put out a glass of water and a notebook, and place your alarm across the room. Tomorrow morning, give yourself ten good minutes before you touch your phone, and see how the day feels when you have chosen its beginning. The first hour is only a small piece of your day, but it is the piece that you can shape.
